1uTRlM6MbMo.tx: If you can conjure up an exciting idea in someone’s mind, you have done something wondrous. A little piece of you has become part of them. Connection, narration, explanation, persuasion, these are all great tools for sharing your ideas. But the most direct way of gifting an idea to an audience is simply to show them. Many talks are anchored like this. You reveal your work to the audience in a way that delights and inspires them. The basic name for this is revelation— the inspiring act of revealing something. In a revelation talk, your goal might just be to create a sense of wonder and delight. If your talk is a demonstration, you're probably hoping to amaze and create a new sense of possibility. If you're sharing a vision of the future, you want it to be so vivid and compelling that your audience makes it their vision. Let’s dig into three kinds of revelation talks. 1. The Wonder Walk. A wonder walk is a talk based on revealing a series of images or wonder moments. It can be like a studio tour with an artist guiding you through each artwork, or a hike with an explorer through a dramatic landscape. Each step is simple, with a sense of wonder building as you move from one piece to the next. This type of talk is often used by artists, designers, photographers, and architects. David Gallo gave a brief talk on underwater astonishments. He showed a series of incredible images and videos of bioluminescent sea creatures. A five-minute talk, it’s been viewed over 15 million times on YouTube. A wonder walk works best with a clear throughline— a connecting idea that links all pieces together. Without that, it can get boring. The goal is to give the audience an inside scoop. Using simple language, share your dreams, your process, and mistakes you made along the way. Illustrator David McAuley shared his drawings of Rome, showing not just the finished works, but his mistakes and dead ends, and how he got from there to the published illustrations. Letting your listeners in on your process is one of the major gifts of any creative talk. Don't just walk people through your work. Take them on a journey that sparks curiosity and inspires new ideas. 2. The Dynamic Demo. If what you’re revealing is not just visual— like new technology or a novel invention— the audience wants to see it in action. Jeff Hahn demonstrated multi-touch technology in 2006, two years before the iPhone. Pranav Mistry demoed Six Sense technology, showing the possibilities when combining a phone, a projector, and a gesture-detecting camera. For a dynamic demo, what matters most is having something impressive to demonstrate. If it's truly compelling, you can excite your audience with a small tease about what they’re about to see. Michael Pritchard started his talk by asking his audience to imagine life without safe drinking water. He poured muddy pond water, sewage runoff, and rabbit droppings into a container, then ran it through his Lifesaver bottle and offered it to an audience member. It tasted fine. He demonstrated that the technology worked, then explained its potential to save lives globally. A typical demo journey is: an initial tease, an explanation or context, the demo itself (visual and dramatic), then the significance— the impact it could have. Exceptional demos can become visions of the future. 3. The Dreamscape. Humans have the unique ability to imagine, invent, innovate, design, and envision worlds that don’t yet exist. We can share these visions, inspiring others to believe and act, and sometimes, turn them into reality. Screenwriters persuade studios to make movies. Inventors persuade companies to build inventions. Architects persuade clients to finance buildings. Businesspeople energize teams with belief in a new vision. Dreams can be communicated with images, demos, sketches, or words. Powerful speeches communicate a dream with inspiring language and passion. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.’s speech at the Lincoln Memorial in 1963 lasted 17 minutes and 40 seconds, yet it changed history. Marine biologist Sylvia Earle used images and compelling language to describe the ocean crisis. She invited the audience to imagine hope spots— protected areas for marine life. One audience member wrote $1 million check on the spot, and protected ocean space has more than tripled since. Sharing a dream effectively requires painting a bold picture of the future and making your audience desire that future. Visual aids can often help with the first part. Architect Thomas Heatherwick included a slide in his TED talk showing an elegant high-rise apartment complex with curved buildings and a park at ground level, painting a future many listeners would be thrilled to inhabit. That's the power of our dreams. They can spread to others. They can build excitement and belief. And through that process, they can come true. Now, Mix and Match. Most talks don’t fit neatly into one category. Select, combine, and adjust talk types to best serve the idea you wish to convey.

h6CmKF-mN2U.tx: Morgan and her twin sister Lisa have been inseparable since birth. So nobody was surprised when they moved into identical houses right next to each other. The only difference? Morgan bought her house, while Lisa is renting hers. For generations, conventional wisdom has been that home ownership is financially better than renting. But let’s follow the twins and see how things play out over the years, based on historical trends in the US. As Morgan and Lisa move into their two-bedroom houses, their upfront costs look a little different. Morgan buys her house for $400,000. Like most buyers, she takes out a mortgage— a loan that she'll pay back to a lender over time with interest. For this, she needs to make a down payment— a lump sum that’s some percentage of the total home price. Between Morgan’s 10% down payment and a few extra fees, known as closing costs, Morgan spends a total of $50,000. Next door, Lisa signs a 12-month lease to rent her house for $1,800 a month. To get her keys, she’ll also pay a security deposit, bringing her total to $3,600— just a fraction of Morgan’s payment. Five years in, Morgan and Lisa have added a few more members to the family. Lisa’s rent has been steadily climbing, about 2% every year. Her monthly rent is now over $2,000, including a new pet fee. This brings her five year total to around $112,000. Meanwhile, Morgan’s still paying off her mortgage, a 30-year loan with a fixed interest rate of 6%. This type of long-term fixed-rate loan is common in the US, though loans with adjustable rates over shorter periods are much more typical in the rest of the world. Longer mortgages lower monthly payments by spreading them over an extended period. Morgan's monthly total, including taxes and insurance, is around $2,500 per month. But a large fraction of early payments goes towards interest. So five years in, she’s spent $150,000 on her property— $38,000 more than Lisa. Despite this, she's only chipped about $25,000 off her mortgage. The good news for Morgan is that the market has changed and interest rates have dropped, allowing her to refinance. Basically, she takes out a new mortgage at the lower interest rate to replace her old one. Her new rate is 5%, bringing her total monthly cost down to around $2,300. 15 years in, Lisa’s rent now exceeds Morgan’s monthly payments. But this isn’t the only cost to consider. During an intense storm season, flash floods hit their neighborhood. As a homeowner, Morgan pays for repairs, while Lisa lets her landlord handle everything. At this point, Morgan has spent over $500,000 on her house, while Lisa has paid around $380,000. After 30 years, Morgan is finally done paying off her mortgage. To get there, she spent about $1 million, including the price of the house, interest, taxes, and insurance. But she's also had to pay for repairs and upkeep, bringing her total to $1.4 million. Meanwhile, Lisa’s rent is now $3,300 a month, and she's spent around $900,000 in rent. But before we calculate final tallies, there’s one more cost to consider: opportunity cost. When Morgan chose to spend $40,000 on a down payment, she missed out on putting that $40,000 into a stable, diversified retirement account. That’s what Lisa did, and it’s grown into $500,000. Morgan’s not sweating it, because her home turned out to be a pretty good investment, as it's now worth $1.3 million. In the end, Morgan spent $1.4 million on a $1.3 million house, putting her at a loss of $100,000. Lisa spent $900,000 in rent, but made $460,000 in investments, putting her at a total loss of $440,000. In this situation, Morgan came out on top. Plus, she’s paid off her mortgage, so she only needs to pay taxes, insurance, and maintenance costs going forward. But Lisa won out in other ways. She had lower monthly expenses for over 10 years, which allowed her to spend on hobbies and travel. In another scenario, she might have put that extra cash into retirement or investments and allowed it to grow. And Lisa wasn't tied to one location. In fact, she just got a job opportunity in a new city and is finally feeling ready to branch out.

G3hXvByzLHs.tx: You can’t give a powerful new idea to an audience unless you can learn how to explain it. Each step builds on what the listener already knows, and metaphors and examples help show how the idea is pieced together. But if explanation is building a brand new idea in someone’s mind, persuasion is something a little more. Persuasion means convincing an audience that their way of seeing something— their perspective— isn’t quite right. That means taking down the parts of their thinking that aren't working and rebuilding something better. Psychologist Barry Schwartz gave a talk that changed the way his audience thinks about choice. Many people are obsessed with maximizing choice; Schwartz sees things differently. He gave a talk on what he calls “the paradox of choice.” Schwartz builds the surprising case that in many circumstances having too many choices actually makes people unhappy. Author Elizabeth Gilbert did something similar. She showed how the power of storytelling can help persuade an audience of a new idea. Her goal was to change the way they thought about creative genius. Instead of imagining genius as something people are born with— either you have it or you don’t— she wanted to persuade her audience to think of it as something people receive as a gift from time to time. Gilbert used her brilliance as a storyteller to persuade her audience of this idea. She also showed them the term “genius” was viewed differently in history. It wasn't always thought of as a thing a person was. It used to be thought of as something that came to them. If you're giving a talk that requires persuading an audience to see something differently, the key is to take the journey one step at a time. Prime your listener’s mind for a change. The philosopher Daniel Dennett uses the term “intuition pump” to refer to any language that makes a new idea seem more believable. In Barry Schwartz’s talk, “Paradox of Choice,” a shopping story he uses is an example of an intuition pump that primes his audience’s mind for a change: So I went to replace my jeans after years and years of wearing these old ones. And I said, “I want a pair of jeans, here’s my size.” And the shopkeeper said, “do you want slim fit, easy fit, relaxed fit? Do you want button fly or zipper fly? You want stonewashed or acid washed? Do you want them distressed? Do you want bootcut? Do you want tapered?” On and on he went. My jaw dropped. And after I recovered I said, “I want the kind that used to be the only kind.” Once an audience has been primed, it’s much easier to make your main argument. Even if it contradicts an idea the audience held true. Another powerful tool is reason. By using reasoning, you can show how and why something is true. Each true assumption leads to a conclusion that must then also be true. Reasoning works using the tool “if, then.” If X is true, then clearly Y must be true. Another kind of reasoned argument is the detective story. Some of the most persuasive TED Talks are set up like detective stories. You start with the big mystery, then travel the world of ideas in search of possible solutions to it, ruling them out one by one, until there’s only one solution left. A simple example is artist Siegfried Woldhek’s talk. He wanted to prove that three famous drawings by Leonardo da Vinci were actually self-portraits da Vinci made of himself at different stages of his life. He started with all of the 120 portraits of males that Leonardo is thought to have made and asks: were any of these self-portraits? Then, like a detective eliminating suspects, Woldhek cut them down. Finally, only three remained. The remaining three portraits are of men of different ages and painted at different times, but they all share the same facial features. And they all match the facial features of a statue— the only known image of da Vinci made by someone else. What makes the detective story persuasive is that we feel as if we have gone on the same learning journey as the speaker. It can sometimes be hard to make reason-based talks really exciting to listen to. Most people can be convinced by reason, but it doesn't always leave them feeling energized. So if you plan to use reason to persuade your audience, you may have to pick up some other tools as well: 1. Inject some humor early on. This says you're going to do some tough thinking, but we're going to have fun. 2. Add an anecdote. You could tell an anecdote that shows how you became interested in the topic you've chosen. 3. Offer vivid examples that ignite the audience’s imagination. 4. Include third-party validation. Pull in the opinions of other people who also believe your idea. Persuasive talks that use reason may be harder for an audience to understand than other talks, and they may not be the most popular. However, they are extremely important. A strong, well-reasoned argument, even if it isn't immediately accepted by everyone, will gradually attract supporters until it becomes unstoppable.

z3Y-gsBKChc.tx: Since 2019, over a thousand imposing warehouse campuses have popped up around the world. Each complex covers nearly 100,000 square meters, uses as much water as a small town, and as much electricity as a small city. These are AI data centers— facilities for running and training Large Language Models like Claude and ChatGPT. We’ve had similar data centers dedicated to operating the internet since the 2000s, but these customized complexes come with a whole new suite of challenges and possibilities. AI data centers are generally organized into several zones. The Network Operations Center manages data traffic and power consumption. Power systems including transformers, gas generators, and battery-powered backups ensure uninterrupted electricity flow. And a connectivity hub called the Meet-Me-Room directs incoming data into the heart of the data center: the server room. When you ask an LLM a question, your prompt enters one of these server rooms. It's too complicated to explore how that model responds right now, but it involves doing tons of math. To manage these calculations, a data center relies on thousands of server racks, each stacked with trays containing server boards that house memory chips and GPUs. These powerhouse microchips use thousands of tiny computing cores working in parallel to do trillions of mathematical operations per second. While most prompts only require a few GPUs to answer, data centers already field tens of thousands of prompts a second. And that rate is growing fast. Plus, training LLMS requires hundreds of thousands of GPUs working together, making server grids like these essential to get an AI up and running. However, all this energy-intensive work leads to a major problem: heat. Even in climate-controlled server rooms, GPUs get hot enough to melt server boards. And the copper wires connecting these chips constantly dissipate energy, using more electricity and generating additional heat. Fortunately, engineers are on the job. To cool chips, they’re using tried-and-true solutions like water towers that absorb and evaporate heat alongside new approaches like piping chilled water behind server boards, or dunking entire trays into non-conductive cooling liquids. At the same time, they're replacing inefficient copper wires that transmit data through electricity with optical fibers that transmit data through light. At the top of many racks, optical transceivers convert electrical data to light signals, which travel through optical fibers with higher data fidelity than copper and near-zero power loss. And as photonics technology gets further integrated inside servers, it can solve another major problem. GPUs only have so much space for copper connections, limiting how much data they transmit at once. But integrated photonic chips can use different wavelengths of light to send multiple streams of data over a few optical lines. This same tech could even let GPUs interact with memory chips on neighboring trays and racks— spreading out their heat load and allowing bigger LLMs to use less power. While some experts believe integrated photonics will reduce data center power use by nearly 50%, this still might not be enough. GPUs run at roughly 16 light bulbs worth of energy. Multiply that by every GPU in a data center, and you're looking at enough energy to power 300,000 homes. Companies are also pursuing ever-smarter AI, which, so far, has meant ever-larger AI. Even with increasing efficiencies, larger models require bigger data centers and more electricity. Some estimates predict that by 2028, US data centers alone could be using as much energy as eight New York Citys. In fact, some AI companies have already proposed pairing next-gen data centers with their own personal nuclear power plant. Clearly, we don’t have enough energy to support this rapid expansion, so we either need to hit the brakes or find ways to compute smarter. For example, while current LLMs are designed to answer every possible question, you don’t need a model that knows Shakespeare to help you fix your dishwasher. We could design topic-specific “small language models” stored in micro-data centers. Alternately, tomorrow’s LLMs might employ new forms of optical computing that cut energy costs by using light itself to do the math. But it won’t matter how efficient these systems get if our hunger for AI keeps increasing. Ultimately, this isn’t a technical problem, it’s a social one: just how many resources are we willing to spend to build smarter machines?

jG7ULeWUfDw.tx: In the early 1900s, physicists Niels Bohr and Hendrika Johanna van Leeuwen separately discovered something shocking. According to every known rule of physics, magnetism was impossible. This finding made no sense. Humans had relied on magnetic compasses for a thousand years, and anyone who had ever held two magnetized metals could tell you that some invisible force was acting on them. Bohr and van Leeuwen knew they were missing something— but what? By the 1920s, physicists had learned quite a bit about the fundamentals of matter. They knew that every material is made of atoms, each comprised of a nucleus containing protons and orbited by electrons. They also knew that both of these particles have a few fundamental properties, including a small amount of mass, an electrical charge, and some amount of magnetism. The origin of these intrinsic properties remains an ongoing mystery. But the result is that every electron and proton is a tiny magnet that works just like their full-size counterparts. Both have invisible magnetic fields that radiate out in closed loops from one end to the other. These magnetic poles are attracted to the dense field lines of the opposite pole of other magnets, and repelled by fields flowing in the opposite direction. Of course, researchers still had questions. What determines the direction of these magnetic fields? And if every atom is composed of tiny magnets, why isn't everything magnetic? The answers emerged with the birth of quantum mechanics: a new branch of physics exploring how the laws of nature work differently at the sub-atomic level. In 1926, a pair of Dutch physicists discovered that— in addition to mass, charge, and magnetism— particles had another fundamental property: quantum spin. This is a confusing label because while nothing is actually spinning, spin does refer to a kind of innate direction that influences a particle’s behavior. And in the 1930s, Nobel Prize laureate John H. Van Vleck discovered that this property held the answer to countless questions about magnetism— including Bohr and van Leeuwen’s. Basically, the direction of a particle’s spin determines the direction of its magnetic field. And since electrons have much stronger magnetic fields than protons, the direction of their spin determines whether or not something is magnetic. If enough of a material's electrons spin in the same direction, their many tiny magnetic fields will align, turning the material into a magnet with a field pointing in that direction. The more aligned electrons, the stronger the magnet. On the other hand, if a material is full of electrons with competing spins their fields cancel each other out, leaving you with something non-magnetic. Most elements have electrons that come in pairs and spin in opposite directions, which is why most materials aren’t magnetic. But iron, nickel, cobalt, and a few rare metals prefer to leave some of their electrons unpaired. This doesn’t automatically make them magnetic— just because their electrons are unpaired doesn’t mean they always spin in the same direction. However, they can be nudged into alignment by interacting with neighboring atoms. And researchers can kick-start this process by applying a strong magnetic field or by heating and cooling the material inside a weaker magnetic field. These metals will stay magnets permanently unless their electrons are scrambled by intense heat or an extremely strong magnetic field. But this magnetization process can make anything magnetic temporarily. Felix Bloch and Edward Mills Purcell took advantage of this in 1945 when they invented nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. This technology uses a strong magnetic field to temporarily align a material's protons, then a weaker field to knock specific molecules out of alignment. The machine then tracks the electromagnetic energy expended by the jostled protons as they realign, allowing researchers to map the material's molecular structure. This invention laid the groundwork for MRI machines, which use a similar approach to magnetize the water in our bodies and map our tissues. Of course, NMR and MRI are just two of countless modern technologies that rely on magnetism. Computer hard drives, electric motors, speakers, wireless communication— all these inventions prove that not only does magnetism exist, but studying this phenomenon remains endlessly attractive.

I8XaYkRW1tA.tx: In July of 2025, top athletes competed in a kilometers-long race— but it had no set path. That's because it was the World Orienteering Championships, and participants equipped with only maps and compasses were expected to find their way between far-off checkpoints at high speeds, weaving between trees, sprinting over rocks, and skirting cliffs. This might sound a little daunting. But whether you identify as a wayfinding whiz or get lost returning from the grocery store, your brain has a built-in navigation system that facilitates spatial skills, from sensing which direction is north to map reading and route learning. It consists of two major parts: the striatum and the hippocampus. The striatum is clued into sensory inputs, like nearby landmarks. With repetition, it comes to associate specific stimuli and actions with certain responses and outcomes, linking these cues with set routes. This forms navigation habits; for example, when you automatically take the same sequence of turns on your way home. The hippocampus, meanwhile, constructs continuous, dynamic mental maps of your environment. It helps you figure out how to get somewhere, even if you've never been or haven't taken that exact route before. Researchers realized the hippocampus’ importance in mental mapping in the 70s, while observing rats’ brain activity and noticing that specific neurons in the hippocampus fired when the rats were in certain spaces. The same thing also happened in complete darkness, indicating that these neurons, which came to be called “place cells,” formed cognitive maps independent of sensory input. It seems that activity in these areas during sleep represents a kind of place replay as the brain consolidates spatial information. And in 2005, researchers discovered additional types of navigational neurons in the region surrounding the hippocampus. This includes “grid cells,” which fire in a regular pattern as one moves, providing the brain with a kind of internal coordinate system. Together, the breakthrough discoveries that put place and grid cells on the map earned the 2014 Nobel Prize. But while the striatum and hippocampus form a navigation system that allows our brains to adapt between strategies depending on the task, we still struggle to find our ways. In the absence of strong external cues, people tend to make small errors that send them off course and into circles. And generally, some of us find ourselves lost more often than others. Most people can handle a striatum-centric, well-practiced route; but those who lean more on hippocampus-forward self-orienting tend to stand out as navigators. Twin studies suggest that genetics account for around 60% of the variation in our navigation abilities. These abilities appear independent of general intelligence, suggesting that navigation is its own distinct cognitive skill. And crucially, research indicates that it’s one that can be practiced and improved. Compared to people from suburban and rural areas, those who grew up in cities— especially ones with more uniform, grid-like layouts— appear to struggle more with navigating less ordered environments. And in a 2010 study, rugby players and martial artists were blindfolded and asked to navigate back to a starting point. The rugby players, who train at much larger scales, did so with more directional accuracy, suggesting that the difference in their spatial training improved their judgement across longer distances. London cab drivers, meanwhile, must learn what’s referred to as “the knowledge,” which consists of extensive routes and landmarks across the city’s infamously complex maze of streets. Those who successfully complete the training have been observed to experience significant hippocampal growth. But the brain’s malleability can be a double-edged sword. While GPS devices reliably get us around, they lead to worse spatial reconstructions than verbal directions and paper maps do. By allowing our brains to engage less actively with environmental cues, GPS may degrade the hippocampal navigation system and impair our own internal sense of direction. So, to help improve it, you can try putting your GPS away on more familiar routes and paying attention to distant landmarks. Last week was my first week back at school as a teacher, and I survived. So last week was my first week back at work after having the summer off, and I survived. I started the week, I did my work. At the end of the week, I felt good, and I had done it. I survived. If I ran a marathon, that's never going to happen. Or if I climbed a mountain, I don't think that's going to happen either. When I finished the race or when I got to the top of the mountain, I could say I did it. Or I … I made it. I would basically be celebrating the fact that I did something extremely difficult. So if you do something very difficult in your life. When you're done, you could say, "I did it," or you could say, "I made it." This third phrase is the phrase, "The worst is behind me now," and you use this phrase usually after you have an injury or surgery or something where part of the experience is really, really bad. QyRqlTV60zM.tx: Imagine a ship struggling in an endless storm. Its captain, though strong and commanding, is a terrible navigator. Neither he nor his crew have been trained to sail, yet they relentlessly vie for control through bribery, flattery, and even mutiny. In the crow's nest sits a true navigator. But her knowledge of the stars, winds, and seasons is dismissed by the crew below. This dysfunctional vessel is the Ship of State— a thought experiment devised by Plato to illustrate his frustration with democracy. Specifically, the kind of democracy practiced in Athens from the 5th to 4th centuries BCE. Unlike the forms of representative democracy practiced today, where voters elect representatives to enact legislation on their behalf, Athenians used a type of direct democracy. While Athenian jurors and most officials were selected by lottery rather than election, every law was voted on directly by the citizens of Athens. Specifically, free men born to Athenian parents— women, foreigners, and enslaved individuals had no voting power. Plato thought this system was destined for ruin. And despite the many differences between Athens’ government and modern representative democracies, many of his fears still ring true today. One of Plato’s two major concerns with direct democracy was its vulnerability to charismatic public speakers. Since laws were voted on in the Assembly, confident orators could sway public opinion for their own benefit. In fact, this kind of speech was considered so powerful a class of paid tutors called sophists emerged to educate wealthy families in the art of persuasion. As a result, Plato felt democracy rewarded the strongest speakers, not those with true political expertise aimed at public welfare. His second concern was democracy's obsession with freedom. In the “Republic,” he outlined how the “license to do whatever one wants” would lead people to prioritize their own desires over the common good. In the short term, Plato believed this would weaken societal cohesion and erode respect for the rule of law. But in the long term, he worried this ever-increasing chaos would lead to a backlash— a yearning for order that would make people vulnerable to a charismatic leader promising stability at the cost of liberty. In Plato’s opinion, all democratic systems were doomed to eventually elect a silver-tongued tyrant who exploits the very freedoms that made democracy possible. Plato’s early solutions to these problems— including handing power to elite philosopher kings— leave much to be desired. But in his final work, “The Laws,” Plato combined democracy and monarchy into a new system he hoped would be stable and enduring. To explain his idea, Plato docked his unruly Ship of State and created a new model: the city of Magnesia. In this imaginary land, everything is designed to counteract the issues of direct democracy, while empowering citizens to be morally and politically engaged. Instead of leaving citizens vulnerable to smooth talkers, Magnesia weaves persuasion directly into its laws. Each law is paired with a “prelude” that outlines the logic behind the law and connects it to shared societal values. For example, Plato feared that false beliefs about the gods would undermine justice. So in Magnesia, atheism and impiety are illegal. But rather than relying solely on the fear of punishment to prevent these crimes, the laws against them contain philosophical arguments designed to convince citizens to adhere to Magnesia’s official religion. Moral education is everywhere in Magnesia, and it’s designed to instill shared responsibility. This way, citizens can retain the individual freedom they value under democracy, but their personal goals are more likely to align with the common good. Even so, Plato still recommends safeguards against corruption. Many of Magnesia’s most powerful positions are held collectively rather than individually. And strict regulations on buying and selling land prevent wealth from pooling in the pockets of an elite minority. Obviously, Magnesia is far from perfect. Plato’s educational regime is borderline cultish, and its constitution requires extremely time-consuming civic engagement from every citizen. Then again, creating an ideal society probably would take time, attention, and education. Your perfect world might not look like Plato’s, but it will likely require a serious commitment from its citizens to guide their Ship of State to a brighter horizon.

-61qDRPG3to.tx: After hours of delay, your red-eye flight is finally boarding, and your long-awaited nap is within reach. But as the line grinds to a halt, you can’t help but think: there must be a faster way to board this plane. You are not alone. Mathematicians have been studying this problem for years, devising a range of different boarding methods and testing them with computer simulations. These models are designed to consider the two biggest plane-loading bottlenecks. The first is seat interference; when someone in a seat closer to the window is blocked by people already in their row. And the second is aisle interference; when passengers seated in the back of the plane are stalled by folks in earlier rows stowing their bags and settling in. Different boarding methods try to tackle these problems in different ways, but the most commonly used approach is called back-to-front boarding. It seems logical— board the back of the plane first so passengers don't need to pass others to reach their seats. And in simulations using a 156-passenger Airbus A320, where every person has a carry-on, back-to-front boarding takes around 23 minutes. Not bad, though it barely outperforms the opposite strategy, boarding front-to-back, suggesting it’s not actually doing much to reduce interference. Other airlines have tried to speed things up by ditching assigned seating altogether, assuming that passengers naturally spread out, easing congestion. Random seating shaves a few minutes off boarding the A320, but it's not perfect. The line tends to slow down at the end as passengers search for remaining seats. And while the freedom might help you avoid a crying toddler, it can also split up groups who board later. To keep assigned seating and further reduce delays, mathematicians developed the outside-in, or WMA method, which loads passengers in window seats first, then middle, and finally aisle seats, bringing boarding time down to just 16.5 minutes. Still, some experts, including astrophysicist Jason Steffen, felt there was room for improvement. Steffen ran countless boarding order simulations until he found the fastest one. His order, aptly named the Steffen Method, can fully board the A320 in just 15 minutes. So why don't airlines use it? Well, Steffen’s method requires passengers to load on in a very specific pattern. First, it fills even rows, then odd rows, using a combination of the WMA and back-to-front methods. By staggering passengers across the cabin, it gives everyone just enough room to load their carry-ons all at once. But Steffen’s method demands perfect execution. Not only does it require all passengers to arrive at the gate on time, but also that they line up in their exact assigned order and be willing to split from their families as they board. While this level of passenger cooperation might seem far-fetched, it's not unprecedented. In the early 1970s, Southwest implemented a policy where planes would land, unload, board, and push back all in under 10 minutes. As soon as the plane touched down, attendants began unloading bags into the aisles. By the time it reached the gate, new passengers were already lined up on the tarmac, boarding as others deplaned. People were still finding seats as the plane taxied toward the runway. Such a system wouldn't fly by today's aviation standards. There are also engineering options to explore. Loading a plane with 240 seats through two doors instead of one can potentially speed up boarding by five minutes. Another proposal, the Side-Slip Seat, offsets the middle seat, allowing the aisle seat to slide over it and temporarily widen the aisle, potentially reducing boarding times by up to 20%. However, while faster boarding times may save airlines on operational costs, it's unlikely they'd actually invest in these redesigns, since there's also value in keeping the process aggravating. Long lines mean passengers are more willing to pay for tickets that allow them to get on the plane first. It’s frustrating. But before you cancel your tickets, it's worth noting that there really isn't much time to be saved. Even the most perfectly executed boarding strategy would likely only save us about ten minutes. So perhaps the best solution is to take a breath, alow your fellow passengers some grace, and try to enjoy the ride.

JhxuP0AuRPA.tx: In 1941, in German-occupied Poland, the Nazis began abducting members of the Jewish population and imprisoning them in extermination camps. But there were exceptions— the Nazis held foreign passport holders in detention camps to be traded later for Germans detained abroad. With this loophole in mind, Aleksander Ładoś, a Polish diplomat in Switzerland, started producing forged Latin American passports and smuggling them to Polish Jews. In the end, these simple paper booklets would mean the difference between life and death for thousands. A striking thing about passports is that they’re actually a relatively new invention. They’re not the first form of travel documents: in ancient Egypt, travelers carried letters of safe conduct issued by rulers; in Han China and Tudor England, foreigners were issued travel passes; and in the 19th century, poorer migrants often needed health certificates to enter the US. However, for much of human history, borders have been relatively fluid and travel lacked bureaucratic requirements. But when World War I broke out in 1914, everything changed. Neighboring countries, and their colonies, became wartime enemies. To deter both espionage and desertion, many European nations established checkpoints at ports of entry to confirm travelers’ nationalities. Here, authorities would screen early versions of passports, which, depending on the issuing country, were documents that followed different formats and contained varying types of information. When the war ended, many expected nations to remove passport requirements. In 1920, the newly established League of Nations discussed this, but in light of other post-war concerns, such as safeguarding national security, preventing the spread of epidemics, and managing the movement of refugees, they opted to temporarily keep the passport system. To ease travel, they encouraged countries to follow international passport guidelines, using booklets of standard size and layout, written in the language of the issuing country and French. But beyond this, every country was free to determine what approvals or documents a person needed to cross its borders. This included rules around issuing visas, the legal permissions dictating how long a person can stay in a country, and what they can do, such as work or study. And by 1926, when the League of Nations met again, the idea of abolishing passports had lost momentum, solidifying the passport system we know today. However, this system brought new problems with it. Passports were used not just to monitor movement, but also as tools of power and control. They reinforced hierarchies between citizens born in colonizer states and those born in the colonies. For example, in the 1920s, UK-born British subjects could get British passports, while Indian-born subjects could receive a distinct British Indian passport. And since passports are issued by governments, they could be withheld from citizens as punishment or to discourage dissent. During the Cold War, the US revoked the passports of political and civil rights activists, like W.E.B. Dubois. As passport monitoring was largely relocated into airports in the second half of the 20th century, advances in digital tracking and databases allowed governments to more tightly regulate and control individual movement. Today, a passport’s strength and where a person can travel to and from are often dependent on relationships between countries. There can be regional agreements, like the Schengen Agreement, which allows border-free travel within 29 European countries. Higher-income countries also typically have better travel access. The result is a system that privileges citizens of certain countries, while constraining others. As of 2025, a US passport holder can enter almost 180 countries without arranging a visa beforehand. For a Pakistani passport holder, that number drops below 40. And these disparities extend to a person’s chances of securing a foreign visa. For example, in 2024, Algerian applicants for US visitor visas faced a much higher refusal rate than Brazilian applicants. In some places, money can buy you access— more than a dozen countries offer "golden passports” programs that grant citizenship, and therefore passports, to people who make a significant investment or donation. As the world becomes increasingly global for some, and increasingly divided for others, the question remains: should lines on a map determine a person’s rights and freedoms?

FBpBUwlDId0.tx: In 1883, American socialite Josephine Cochrane was suddenly widowed and left with mounting debts. But she had an idea she hoped would turn her fortunes around. Years of hosting lavish dinner parties and watching her dishware get chipped during handwashing convinced her the world needed a better way to clean dishes. So, she poured the little money she had left into building a prototype, eventually showcasing her dishwashing contraption at the Chicago World's Fair. This was the first step towards the modern dishwasher, whose basic design remains remarkably similar to Cochrane's. When you press start on a dishwasher, it fills a small basin with water that's heated up to 60°C. Then the pre-wash cycle begins. A circulation pump sends high-pressure water up into spray arms, where it shoots out of angled nozzles, propelling the arms to spin. The water recollects in the basin, where, in most modern models, a turbidity sensor measures the water’s dirtiness by seeing how much light passes through it. The dishwasher then adjusts the wash time and water temperature accordingly and transitions to the wash cycle. Detergent is released and the dishwasher cycles the now-detergent-filled water. This dirty water drains and clean water, heated to an even hotter 68°C, is circulated for a final sanitizing rinse. This is at least 10 degrees warmer than a typical sink’s hottest water, and hot enough to eliminate most foodborne bacteria. Finally, the dishwasher may enter an optional drying cycle. While that's how most dishwashers work, how well they actually clean depends on several factors— the first being the type of detergent you use. Detergent comes in three forms: liquid, powder, and pods. The main ingredient in all three is the surfactant. These special dual-ended molecules remove food residues by latching onto them with one end and pulling towards the water with the other. You'll also find surfactants in regular dish soap, but detergents go further. They often contain enzymes that break down food into smaller pieces that surfactants can easily tug away, and bleach, which disinfects and removes stains. So, which detergent form is best? Liquid detergent can only contain bleach or enzymes, since bleach breaks down enzymes in liquid form. Powder detergents solve this problem by coating powdered enzymes with a protective wax, allowing them to work alongside powdered bleach. But even more effective are dishwasher pods that separate components using a plastic film. Though, pods may have environmental impacts— some studies claim the plastic biodegrades in a couple of months, while others find it persists for much longer. How you treat your dishwasher, and the dishes you put in, can also affect performance. A dirty dishwasher or filter can trick the turbidity sensor into thinking dishes are dirtier than they are, prompting an unnecessarily long wash cycle. And while it might seem counterintuitive, rinsing dishes beforehand can also cause problems. If dishes are well rinsed, the turbidity sensor will detect minimal grime and trigger a short wash cycle, which may not be enough to break down any stubborn stuck-on crust. Further, the enzymes in detergent are designed to latch onto food residue, so the best practice is to simply scrape your dishes before loading. What’s more, by letting the dishwasher do all the work, you'll also save water. Dishwashers recycle water during the wash cycle, so they only use 3 to 5 gallons. That’s equivalent to running a kitchen sink for up to 2.5 minutes. So if you think handwashing your dishes might take longer than that, it might be worth just running a load. Of course, there are reasons to not throw in the towel on handwashing altogether. Since dishwashers use very hot water, they can warp wooden items and certain plastics, damaging seals in travel mugs or storage containers. Sharp knives can also be dulled by detergents, or they can even damage the dishwasher itself. And there's also an energy consideration. On average, a standard dishwasher cycle uses about the same amount of energy as leaving your TV on for 12 hours. Clearly, there are situations when handwashing makes more sense. But if you’re faced with a dinner party’s worth of dishes, a dishwasher can be a welcome reprieve.

JDqpcHGfJ2I.tx: Deep in the jungles of southeast Asia lurks a deadly creature with sharp teeth and a venomous bite: a slow loris. Despite their wide-eyed looks, their story is much fiercer than you might imagine. Lorises split off from other primates as far back as 70 million years ago, when T-rexes still roamed. And they gradually migrated from Africa to Asia. Around sunset each evening, lorises get active, moving slowly and deliberately through the trees in their home range. They use their large eyes to scan their surroundings for their next meal and take little time to rest. Pygmy lorises, for one, regularly pass their nights in near-constant motion. Unlike many other primates, however, slow lorises have a higher proportion of slow-twitch muscle fibers, which are favored for long-winded exertion versus speedy spurts. They also have extra vertebrae, making them especially flexible. When needed, slow lorises can stay still, gripped to one tree branch for hours, extra blood vessel networks in their limbs preventing them from weakening or becoming numb. Their slow movements help them go undetected. And that way, they avoid threats, staying stealth around predators that tend to be on the lookout for motion; and they can better hunt unsuspecting prey. Slow lorises are omnivores that go after lots of insects and other small animals, as well as fruit and nectar. Interestingly, they also consume a lot of tree gum and sap, scratching at tree bark with a row of specialized teeth called a “toothcomb.” Though these plant substances are tough to digest, slow lorises seem to be well-equipped to detoxify them. Some scientists even suspect that they sequester the toxins from the tree gum they devour because slow lorises are, in fact, toxic themselves. They’re the only venomous primates, and one of only a few venomous mammals. And their venom system is thought to be one of the most complex in the animal kingdom. It works in two parts, with the combination of two separate secretions. When threatened, slow lorises may assume their venom pose, raising their arms so they can easily access glands near their armpits that secrete a toxic oil. When they lick at the glands, the oil combines with their saliva to form their formidable, flesh-rotting venom. They store the mixture on their sharp toothcomb, to be deployed with a bite capable of causing intense pain, tissue damage, anaphylaxis, and, in small animals, even death. Slow lorises spread the oil over their coats where it can kill parasites on contact. In fact, the number of parasites they carry on their skin and fur is remarkably low relative to other primates. And it may also be protective against bigger threats. When slow lorises sleep, they curl into little balls, toxic coats exposed, perhaps to help deter predators. Cats, sun bears, and civets are repelled by just the scent of slow loris saliva— though orangutans seem to have found a way around it. The most common victims of slow loris bites, however, are other slow lorises. Tracking one population over the course of eight years, scientists only recorded one slow loris dying from natural predation. But 20% of them got bitten by other slow lorises, perhaps in fights over limited territory. And while they may look cute to us, those same features might send a very different message to predators at dusk. When in danger, slow lorises may assume their venom pose, sway, and make a raspy noise. Some scientists think these behaviors and their markings might help them effectively mimic spectacled cobras. This could be an example of Müllerian mimicry, where one dangerous species benefits from sharing certain characteristics with another, helping warn other creatures to stay away. But if slow lorises evolved to look like cobras, we don't seem to be getting the memo. ikrTNUvEDbw.tx: Hello, hello! Welcome or welcome back! I’m Jean, and today I’m going to teach you how to introduce yourself. You can probably already introduce yourself a little bit. If I say, “What’s your name?” What do you say? You probably said, “My name is…” or “I’m…” These two phrases are all you need to give your name. The only difference between them is that “My name is” can be a little bit more formal, but that’s not a rule. You can choose “My name is” or “I’m” or switch between them—whichever you prefer. But what if your full name isn’t what you prefer? Or what if your name is really long and you want people to call you by a nickname? Here are a few ways you can tell someone your preferred name. “I go by…” “I prefer…” “You can call me…” So, let’s say you have a really long first name, like Alexander or Alexandra. Maybe you want everyone to call you “Alex” instead. So here’s one way that conversation can go: “Hi! How are you? What’s your name?” “I’m Alexandra, but you can call me Alex.” “Nice to meet you, Alex.” Now let’s go over the top 5 most common questions someone can ask you and ways you can answer them. Number 1: Where are you from? Here are some options you can use to answer this question. You can say, “I’m from {country}.” For example, I’m from the United States. Or, I could also say, I’m from America. You can say, “I’m from {country}, specifically {state/city}.” For example, I’m from the United States, specifically Florida. But “from” can be a little confusing—does it mean where you live or where you were born? It can mean either. If you want to tell this to someone, you can say something like this: “I live in {current city/country}, but I’m originally from {birth city/country}.” OR “I live in {current city/country}, but I was born in {birth city/country}.” OR you can switch the order of these phrases. You can say, “I was born in {birth city/country} but right now I’m living in {current city/country}.” For example, I was born in Kentucky, but right now I’m living in Florida. Number 2: What do you do? This question is asking what your current job is. Here are some ways to answer this question: You can say, “I’m a {job title}.” For example, I’m a teacher. If you are the only person who does your job in your company or organization, then you can probably say, “I’m the {job title}.” For example, I’m the principal of this school or I’m the CEO of this company. If you don’t currently have a job, you can say, “I’m currently unemployed” or “I’m currently looking for work.” Number 3: How long have you been learning English? This question is a great opportunity to practice a common mistake: for vs since. Here are some ways to answer this question: You can say, “I have been learning English for {an amount of time}.” For example, I have been learning English for three years. OR You can say, “I have been learning English since {a specific date}.” For example, I have been learning English since 2022. We use “for” with an amount of time, like for two seconds for five minutes for six hours for two weeks for a month etc. We use “since” with a specific time, like since two o’clock since last week since then since January since I was eight years old Number 4: Why are you learning English? Of course, why you are learning English is personal to you, but here are a few options: You can say, “I’m learning English for school/work.” Or, you can say, “I’m learning English just for fun.” For example, I’m learning Spanish because a lot of people speak Spanish in my city. Number 5: What other languages do you speak? If you speak your native language and you’re only learning English, you can say: “Just {native language.}” Of course, if you speak a lot of languages, you can say: “My native language is {language} but I also speak {other languages}.” If you want to say how well you can speak another language, here’s how you can say that: “I can understand a little {language}.” “I can speak a little {language}.” “I can have a conversation in {language}.” “I’m fluent in {language}.” For example, My native language is English, but I can have simple conversations in French and Mandarin Chinese and I can understand and speak a little Spanish. Here’s a bonus question: how old are you? In American society in general, it’s usually not a good idea to ask a woman how old she is, but here are some options. You can say, “{number}.” For example, 31. You can say, “I’m {number}.” For example, I’m 31. You can say, “I’m {number} years old.” For example, I’m 31 years old. Or, if you don’t want to use a specific number, you can say: “I’m in my early/mid/late twenties, thirties, forties, etc.” For example, I’m in my early thirties. Here are two common mistakes I often hear: “I’m {number} years.” and “I have {number} years.” These are mistakes in standard English. You can say “I’m {number}” or “I’m {number} years old” but not “I’m {number} years.” And we don’t use “have” in English to talk about age. Congratulations! You now have the tools to introduce yourself. Here’s an example of using all of these sentences together. Hi! I’m Jean. You can call me Miss Jean. I’m from the United States, specifically Florida. I live in Florida, but I was born in Kentucky. I’m an English teacher. I’ve been teaching English since 2019. I’m teaching English because I love languages and helping people. English is my native language, but I can have simple conversations in French and Mandarin Chinese and I can understand and speak a little Spanish. According to the original hypothesis, Toba’s volcanic winter lasted as long as 10 years and its impacts lasted as much as 1,000 years. Based on those numbers, of course it could cause a global catastrophe. But as volcanologists have continued to study Toba… and archeologists have continued to study the lives of ancient humans… both fields have found that the evidence just isn’t there. I mean, a super eruption definitely occurred. But studies of the sediment from that time don’t show any hints of major long term cooling. Studies tracking … a ton of sulfur dioxide. The truth is studying large volcanic eruptions from this long ago is just really hard to do. And our understanding of these systems is going to change drastically over time as the technology to do our research improves. There’s a lot of inaccurate information out there about super eruptions, but the truth can actually be way more interesting than the stuff people make up. And I’m personally really grateful that we probably don’t have to worry about super eruptions in our lifetime, even if it would mean I don’t have to worry about saving for retirement if we had one.

Welcome to today's special episode, which is dropping on April 1st, a day known as April Fool's Day here in the United States. Let's dive into this quirky tradition–quirky meaning unusual in an amusing way–that might seem a bit weird if you're not familiar with it! So what exactly is April Fool’s Day? It’s a day to play jokes on people, like the one I played on you just now when I said I wasn’t going to make any more English Extras episodes. You might be wondering: how in the world did we come to have this tradition? Well, first thing’s first: nobody really knows exactly where this tradition came from. There are some fun theories floating around, like one involving King Charles IX of France changing the day of the new year. But the mystery remains! It's technically on your calendar, but it's not a “real” holiday, like Christmas or Easter. You'll still be going to work or school, but with one big difference: you've got to keep your guard up! To keep your guard up means to stay alert and be careful about potential tricks or dangers, and that is certainly necessary on a day like April Fool’s Day. I’ll explain why. On April Fool's Day, your friends, family, and/or coworkers might try to trick you. One of the ways we say this in English is “to pull a prank on someone.” This means trying to make someone believe something that isn't true, usually just for a bit of fun. Pranks can be small and create “ha-ha, very funny” type of responses, or they can be more elaborate (meaning “complicated”) and potentially not so funny for the victim. Now, I'll be honest with you: I'm not a big fan of pranks. Why? Because they can quickly turn into this never-ending cycle. One person tricks another, then they get tricked back, and suddenly everyone's just trying to one-up each other! To one-up someone is to do something slightly better than someone else, and that can create a cycle that never ends when it comes to pranks. And pranks can go wrong! Pranks can be difficult to do well. The goal is supposed to be a little harmless fun, but sometimes they can hurt people emotionally or even physically, if it goes wrong. The victim of the prank is often the only one not laughing. Of course, there are many pranks that are harmless, as they should be, in my opinion. Like my little joke at the beginning of this episode about stopping English Extras - see? No harm done! The magic words that reveal a prank is “April Fools!” It's like saying “Just kidding!” but only on this specific day. When someone says “April Fools!”, it means “Gotcha!” Gotcha is an informal way of saying “I got you!” or also “I understand.” So when you pull a prank, after you can say, “Gotcha!” or “April Fools!” and that tells the other person that it was a prank, a joke. And it's not just regular people who love this day. Businesses can also get in on the fun, creating ridiculous fake announcements or products. For example, in 2015, you could go to com.google and it was a mirror image of Google search results. Apparently, it created a somewhat nauseating effect. Also in 2015, Amazon changed its homepage to the same style it had in 1999, which is actually really cool in my opinion because it shows just how far our web style has come. Keep an eye out for any changes on April 1st. If something crazy happens, take it with a grain of salt. It might just be a prank and you never know what someone is going to do. If you want to join in the fun, here are some totally harmless prank ideas: You can try giving someone a “chocolate-covered strawberry” that's actually a brussel sprout covered in chocolate. (Don’t do this if the person is allergic to brussel sprouts.) You can try putting a tiny piece of tape over the sensor on someone’s computer mouse. Or you can try replacing the sugar with salt before someone gets their morning coffee. Do any of these at your own risk!
